Real fields supply the marked point: software severity scoring calls it High, clinical grading calls it Grade 3, the nuclear event scale calls it level 4. The project's 0.7 is not such a point.
task:B144.why: Two independent results, and the second is the one that settles it. First, a constraint solver confirms that a re-scaling which preserves the order of every single pair can still change how many findings sit above a fixed value of 0.7, while the same attack on a cut named by a marked point of the ordering has no solution at all. Second, on the archive's own 3,170 recorded severities, multiplying every one of them by 0.6993 - which reorders nothing, with a rank correlation of exactly 1 and an exhaustive pairwise check clean - destroys 1,416 of 1,416 critical calls, the whole of them. So every critical judgement the project has ever made can be erased by a change of units that alters no ordering. A free panel round measured the same thing from the other side: carried linearly into the 4 validated scales, 0.7 lands exactly on a recognised boundary in 1 of them and between levels in the other 3. And a third part of the finding is sharper still, because 174 of those 1,416 critical calls are decided by a tie at a boundary whose value is not even 0.7 in the real numbers.
task:B144.evidence_line: By syntax tree on the reference runner: 1 command-line domain argument defaulting to software, 0 functions that classify a domain from task content, and 0 of 67 archived run states recording any domain at any depth. 0 of 20 domain configuration files declare a severity scale or a critical level, Wilson [0.000000, 0.161125], Clopper-Pearson [0.000000, 0.168433]. On the archive, 1,416 of 1,416 critical calls destroyed by an order-preserving re-scaling, 1.000000, Wilson [0.997294, 1.000000], Clopper-Pearson [0.997398, 1.000000], counted on 2 independent routes that agree exactly. 174 of 1,416 sit exactly on the cut, 0.122881, Wilson [0.106795, 0.141009]. Verified on 6 routes: SymPy, z3, exact rational arithmetic, mpmath, NumPy and Wolfram Language.
options: DECLARE THE SCALE AND THE CRITICAL LEVEL IN EACH DOMAIN CONFIGURATION, AND RECORD THE RESOLVED DOMAIN IN THE RUN STATE. This is the recommendation. Neither half removes the existing cut or changes what the gate admits today; they make it possible to ask, for the first time, what the cut means in the domain a run was actually conducted in. Nothing can route to a scale while nothing classifies the domain and nothing records it, so the recording is prior to any later change.
DECLARE THE SCALES ONLY and leave the run state as it is, accepting that a finished run cannot afterwards be told which scale it was judged on, so the declaration cannot be audited against anything.

CHANGE NOTHING UNTIL AFTER THE RUNWAY, on the grounds that the cut is operationally inert on the computed severity - moving it from 0.7 to 0.95 reclassifies 0 archived entries - and that the live harm is therefore bounded. This is a defensible reading and its cost is that the 1,416 critical calls already in the archive stay uninterpretable.
task:B144.recommendation_standards: Option 1 is ADDITIVE on both halves: no scale is removed, the 0.7 cut stays exactly where it is, and both changes add a declaration where today there is none - 0 of 20 configurations and 0 of 67 run states. It is the SIMPLEST SUFFICIENT change, because the alternative that would actually bite, replacing the cut, is a change to what the gate admits and is yours rather than mine. It is NOT COMPOSED in the sense your standard requires: the declaration and the recording are independent of one another, no measurement shows the pair dominating either part alone on a named property, and so each stands or falls on its own.

task:B154.title: B154 - 2 decisions from the encoding work: where the failure-mode critical level sits, and whether 22 draft boxes go to the panel
task:B154.spoken_heading: WHETHER THE ENGINEERING CRITICAL LEVEL MOVES FROM 7 TO 9 TO MATCH THE PUBLISHED SAFETY LINE, AND WHEN THE 22 NEW DRAFT ENCODINGS GO TO THE PANEL
task:B154.what: 2 decisions came out of the encoding work of the 11th and 12th of November, and neither blocks any other item, so both are reported rather than raised as blockers. The first is where the critical level sits on the engineering severity scale. The engineering domain now declares the AIAG-VDA failure-mode severity scale, whose published landmarks are 7 to 8 for high consequence and 9 to 10 for safety or regulatory consequence. The manifest declares the critical level at 7. The second is the 22 new expert encodings written against current published standards, all of them tagged DRAFT, which were authorised for panel adjudication in the morning.
task:B154.why: On the first: 7 is the conservative cut, because it admits MORE findings as critical than the standard's own safety line would. Moving it to 9 would align the declaration with the standard it cites, and would LOOSEN what the gate admits. A change that loosens a gate changes which findings reach a human, so it is not a change to take from a reading of a standard. On the second: the tier ladder is DRAFT, then CROSS_VERIFIED, then VALIDATED by a human, then OPERATIONAL. A panel moves a box exactly 1 rung, to CROSS_VERIFIED, and not to the top; the human validation rung stays separate and stays his. All 22 are tagged DRAFT on purpose so that 142 lines of detail is never mistaken for adjudicated authority, because density is not provenance.
task:B154.evidence_line: Measured on the 12th of November from the manifest itself: the severity scale is declared for 10 of 10 domains and the critical level for 4 of 10, the other 6 declaring no scale with a stated reason and inheriting from the application domain. 3 of the 4 declared scales were corrected against their published standards during this work: CVSS version 4.0 and not 3.1, GHS Revision 11 with 5 categories and not 4, and the AIAG-VDA failure-mode scale with both of its landmark levels named rather than 1. CTCAE version 5.0 was confirmed as already correct.
options: LEAVE THE ENGINEERING CRITICAL LEVEL AT 7 AND SEND THE 22 DRAFT ENCODINGS TO THE PANEL AT HIS CONVENIENCE. This is the recommendation. 7 is the conservative cut and nothing is lost by holding it: a finding admitted as critical that turns out not to be gets a second look, while a finding excluded by a looser cut gets none. The panel dispatch costs nothing on the free seats and moves the 22 boxes exactly 1 rung.

MOVE THE ENGINEERING CRITICAL LEVEL TO 9 TO MATCH THE PUBLISHED SAFETY AND REGULATORY LINE. This is defensible and it is what the standard's own text says, but it loosens the gate, so the consequence of being wrong falls on findings that would no longer reach a human at all.

HOLD THE PANEL DISPATCH UNTIL THE 28 OLDER ENCODINGS ARE ENRICHED, SO THE PANEL SEES AN EVEN CORPUS. Defensible, and it delays adjudication of 22 boxes that are already written and already in use by the composer. The 22 would stay DRAFT meanwhile, which is the correct state for them, so the cost is time rather than risk.
task:B154.recommendation_standards: Option 1 is SIMPLEST SUFFICIENT: it changes nothing that is working and asks only for a dispatch that was already authorised. It is ADDITIVE on both halves, because no scale is removed, no encoding is withdrawn, and the declaration at 7 stays exactly where it is while the panel adds a tier rung to 22 boxes that currently have none. COMPOSABILITY is NOT claimed here and the word is used deliberately: options 1 and 3 could be composed, but no measurement shows the composed form dominating either part alone on any named property, and under the project's own definition a composed fix may be recommended only with such a measurement. Where a single fix performs as well, the single fix is preferred.

task:B160.title: B160 - the figure the turn hook prints to him rests on a proxy no sibling predicate agrees with on any entry it applies to
task:B160.spoken_heading: WHICH TEST REPLACES THE PROXY THAT DECIDES WHETHER A QUESTION WAS ASKED AFTER YOU ALREADY RULED, SINCE 3 CANDIDATES DISAGREE ON EVERY ENTRY THEY APPLY TO
task:B160.what: Every turn prints a line saying how many open items await your ruling. For an item that already carries a ruling of yours, the test deciding whether anything is still owed is whether ANY date anywhere in that item's text is later than the ruling date. The intent behind it is exact and correct: a question raised after a ruling cannot have been answered by it. The implementation is a stand-in for that intent, and a dated progress note of mine is not a question. 3 tests for the same idea were computed side by side. The first is the one in use. The second asks whether a later date sits inside the asking sentence itself. The third asks whether an asking sentence is positioned after the first post-ruling date.
task:B160.why: They disagree on all 4 of the items they apply to, and not 1 of the 4 gets the same answer from all 3. The convergence gate item is yes, no, yes. The difficulty estimator item is yes, yes, no. The verified-flag item is yes, no, no. The joint-round item is yes, yes, no. The line you read says 8 of 12 open items await you, and 4 of those 8 are these. If the test in use is wrong, that figure is wrong, and the defensible floor is 4 rulings you have never given plus 4 permissions. No 4th test was written, deliberately, on this project's own rule that a surface defeating 3 predicates is the point to stop and raise it rather than to try a 5th time.
task:B160.evidence_line: Measured on the 12th of November from the task list itself: 3 predicates disagree on 4 of 4 ruled items awaiting a ruling, 1.000000, Wilson 95 per cent [0.510109, 1.000000], Clopper-Pearson [0.397635, 1.000000]. Separately, 4 of 12 open items carry no recorded ruling at all, 0.333333, Wilson [0.138120, 0.609378], and 6 of 12 were raised on or after the 10th of November, 0.500000, Wilson [0.253782, 0.746218].
options: LEAVE THE TEST AS IT IS AND CHANGE NOTHING. This is the recommendation. It errs toward telling you about an item rather than hiding it, and the suppression direction is the one this project has already had to withdraw once, on the 9th of November, after retiring asking sentences removed live questions from your list. The cost is that the printed figure can overstate what you owe, which a report can say in words instead.

REPLACE IT WITH THE SENTENCE TEST, so an item is treated as awaiting you only when a later date sits inside the asking sentence itself. This would move the verified-flag item and the convergence gate item off your list, leaving 6 of 12 rather than 8. It is the tightest of the 3 and the most likely to hide something.

REPLACE IT WITH THE POSITION TEST, so an item is treated as awaiting you only when an asking sentence sits after the first post-ruling date. This would move 3 of the 4 off your list, leaving 5 of 12. It reads a document as if it were chronological, which these entries are not.

KEEP THE TEST AND REPORT THE DISAGREEMENT BESIDE THE COUNT, so the line says 8 and the report names the 4 that 3 tests cannot agree on. Nothing is hidden and nothing is overstated without a note, at the cost of a longer line.
task:B160.recommendation_standards: Option 1 is ADDITIVE in the strict sense: it removes no capability and keeps the bias toward telling you. Options 2 and 3 are REMOVALS of items from your decision list, and the additive standard permits a removal only on a committed measurement showing the replacement dominates on a named property; no such measurement exists, because the 3 predicates disagree rather than one of them being shown correct. Option 4 is a COMPOSITION of option 1 with a new report line, and composability requires a measurement showing the pair beats either part alone, which has not been taken; it is named because it may be what you want, not because the standard currently licenses it. SIMPLEST SUFFICIENT favours option 1, since the overstatement can be corrected in prose at no risk to the stop gate.
